recommendations.text: Taking account of the various national legal texts, to ensure that a more consistent approach is adopted by the districts on the development of their inspection programmes (Article 7 of Directive 91/630/EEC and Article 8 of Directive 1999/74/EC).

In relation to laying hens farms, take measures to ensure that: (a) Consideration is given to the use of further characters in the identification number with the purpose of distinguishing single flocks kept in separated buildings of the same 11 establishment (Point 2.3 of the Annex to Directive 2002/4/EC). (b) Farms with a transitional period complete the necessary upgrading by 1.5.2007 (Decision 2004/433/EC).

In relation to checks of holdings with pigs: (a) Follow-up visits are prioritised and carried out in a timely manner. In relation to slaughterhouses: (a) Provide confirmation that commitments previously given, to replace the system for stunning cattle with methods which fulfil Article 3 and Annex C(II)(3)(A) of Directive 93/119/EC in each of the slaughterhouses where single-electrodes were used, have been fully implemented. audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should consider strengthening implementation of controls of the uses of plant protection products in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should continue with the revision of the labels to ensure that all labels of PPPs are in compliance with Directive 1999/45/EC of the European Parliament and the Council on classification, packaging and labelling of dangerous preparations.
The competent authorities should consider following SANCO Guideline Document 223/2000, rev. 9 concerning parallel imports when legislation is amended.
The competent authorities should arrange the safe destruction of obsolete pesticides in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment.

The competent authorities should consider increasing the number of samples taken and the number of analytes examined for pesticide residue analysis so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and to ensure adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC as amended.
The competent authorities should consider progressing with the validation of methods for the analysis of pesticide residues. 20
The competent authorities should ensure the enforcement of MRLs specified by Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC, as amended, by using analytical method with the required sensitivity.

The competent authorities should consider taking full account of the Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residues Analysis Document No. SANCO/10476/2003, particularly with respect to calibration. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation.

audits.title: Potato Audit

recommendations.text: The State Plant Protection Service is kept informed of genetic Solanum material held in the country as required in point 18.4 of Annex IV, Part A, Section II of Council Directive 2000/29/EC;
Before material is released from the gene bank, it has been tested for all organisms mentioned in point 18.3 of Annex IV, Part A, Section II of Council Directive 2000/29/EC;
Lots with a "suspected" occurrence of ring rot are handled in compliance with Article 4, point 2 of Council Directive 93/85/EEC;
Disinfection of equipment and storage is imposed immediately after the outbreak and at least again the following year as required in the revised Council Directive 93/85/EEC, Annex IV, point 4.1(c);
A proactive and systematic investigation of possible clonal links to sister lots in Latvia is carried out as required in Article 6 of Council Directive 93/85/EEC;

A list of potato varieties recognised as resistant to potato cyst nematodes is prepared and communicated to the Commission each year as required in Article 10 of Council Directive 69/465/EEC. The Single authority in Latvia should consider:
Increasing the survey intensity for ring rot in the ware potato sector. The substantial part of potatoes being produced by the small, unregistered producers should also be represented in the survey;
Extending the survey for R. solanacearum to include surface water and wild hosts; 21

To have potato varieties tested for resistance against a range of potato cyst nematode pathotypes. To ensure intensive hunting and further monitoring of wildlife for rabies incidence in the infected areas.
To follow the recommendations of the SCAHAW report concerning vaccination strategy and the storage and distribution of vaccine.
To introduce a control system on the maintenance of the cold chain for the vaccine.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the characteristics of the vaccine used are in line with the 6th and 7threcommendations of the SCAHAW report on oral vaccination of foxes against rabies, and the 1st recommendation of the notes on the meeting of the rabies subgroup of the Task Force for monitoring disease eradication programmes in the Member States; be prepared in case an unfavourable outcome of quality controls leads to disruption of the vaccination campaign;

Ensure that relevant data are collected and analysed after each oral rabies vaccination campaign, in order to monitor and ensure its efficacy, as per the 1st recommendation of the SCAHAW report on oral vaccination of foxes against rabies, and the 3rd and 4th recommendation of the Task Force report;
Type the rabies virus strains collected in the field (4th recommendation of the SCAHAW report on oral vaccination of foxes against rabies and 5th recommendation of the Task Force report);
Consider the reduction of the flight distance for aerial distribution of baits (19th recommendation of the SCAHAW report on oral vaccination of foxes against rabies, and of the Task Force report);

Develop, detail and adapt the contingency plans at national and regional level in order for them to be immediately and efficiently applicable in order to allow access to facilities, equipment, personnel and all other appropriate materials necessary for the rapid and efficient eradication of the outbreak, as per Article 62 (2) of Directive 2005/94/EC, Article 72 (2) of directive 2003/85/EC, Article 21 (1) of Directive 2002/60/EC, Article 22 (1) of Directive 2001/89/EC, Article 18 (1) of Directive 2000/75/EC, Article 21 (1) of Directive 92/66/EEC, Article 17 (1) of Directive 92/35/EEC; ensure that permanently operational expert groups are set up so that they can assist the CA in ensuring the disease preparedness, as required by Article 23 (5) of Directive 2001/89/EC, Article 22 (5) of Directive 2002/60/EC, and Article 78 of Directive 2003/89/EC; in particular, and in accordance with this last article, ensure that they arecomposed of epidemiologists, veterinary scientists and virologists in a balanced way

Ensure that updates and revision of contingency plans are performed as necessary,and that significant modifications or updated plans are submitted to the Commission at least every 5 years, as per Article 62,5 of Directive 2005/94/EC, Article 72,10 of directive 2003/85/EC, Article 21,3 of Directive 2002/60/EC, Article 22,3 of Directive 2001/89/EC;

Ensure that diagnostic procedures, sampling and laboratory testing is performed in accordance with the Community diagnostic standards and requirements, as per Article 50,1 of directive 2005/94/EC, Article 17,1 of Directive 2003/89/EC, Article 18,1,a of Directive 2002/60/EC, Article 17,1,a of Directive2001/89/EC, Article 12 of Directive 82/66/EC, and that a national reference laboratory is formally designated for all diseases, including AHS (Article 14 of Directive 92/35/EEC) and ASF (Article 18,1,b of Directive 2002/60/EC), and details are available to the other Member States and to the public;

Ensure that alert drills and simulation exercises are performed at the adequate frequency, as required in Article 73,1 of Directive 2003/85/EC, Annex VI, (f), (ii) to Directive 2002/60/EC, Annex VII, g, (ii) to Directive 2001/89/EC, and submit the main results on the FMD exercises to the Commission, as required in Article 73,3 of Directive 2003/89/EC;

Improve the traceability of cattle by enforcing the movement information to be recorded in the passports (as required by Article 7 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2004, and Article 6 (1) (c) of Regulation (EEC) No 911/2004, and by ensuring a rapid registration of movement notifications in the national database so that it can effectively its role as described in Article 14 (C) (3) of Directive 64/432/EEC;

Ensure that the disinfectants to be used, and their concentrations, are officially authorised and registered to ensure the destruction of the specific agents against which they are intended to be used, as per Article 48 (e) of Directive 2005/94/EC, Article 11,1 of Directive 200389/EC, Article 12 (a) of Directive 2002/60/EC, Article 12,1,a of Directive 2001/89/EC, Article 11 (a) of Directive 92/66/EEC, Article 16 (1) (a) of Directive 92/119/EEC; to ensure that the disinfectants labels bear the authorisation number allocated by the CA and the expiry date, as required by Article 20 (3) (b) and (i) of Directive 98/8/EC;

Consider reviewing the provisions for financial compensation in case of compulsory killing or slaughter of animals in case of contingency, so that they do not represent an impediment for an efficient application of such measures;

Ensure that the premises in slaughterhouses and assembly centres meet the structural requirements aimed at avoiding contamination in case of animal health risk (Article 11 (1) (c) and (d) of Directive 64/432/EEC; Annex III, Chapter II (1) (a) and (b) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004); to ensure that animals are accepted in assembly centres and certified only if they are correctly identified, and on the basis of an official document containing all necessary information completed by the official veterinarian for the holding of origin, as required by Articles 5 (2) (a) and 11 (1) (e)of Directive 64/432/EEC.

citations.text: The audit team visited a holding using Article 3b derogation and noted: The permit to move pigs from this holding to slaughterhouses was issued quarterly (five separate movement permits were available as the holding supplied five different abattoirs and each movement permit requires a route plan). The audit team reviewed movements of pigs into this herd for the period January to March 2018 and confirmed all pigs originated from a single, separate breeding holding. recommendations.text: With regard to hunting premises, to ensure that arrangements are put in place to ensure the effectiveness of the official controls (Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625) established in the ASF Eradication Plan (elaborated in accordance with Article 16 of Directive 2002/60/EC).

citations.text: Since February 2019, the FVS has been responsible for the control of wild boar carcases in processing rooms and storage facilities of hunting grounds (chillers, freezers or other equipment), where wild boar carcases are stored while ASF test results are awaited. To date, the FVS does not have an overview of the facilities available for each hunting ground. When the FVS started to carry out official controls on hunting grounds, they set, mainly due to staff constraints, an objective for 2019 of inspecting 10% of the hunting grounds (the same objective of 10% for 2020), and a minimum number of carcases based on a statistical approach. From March to December 2019, 190 hunting grounds were inspected. The visits targeted either the bigger hunting grounds or the ones with a higher number of hunted animals, although the competent authorities expected a higher percentage of non-compliances linked to the lack of adequate storage facilities for carcases in the smaller hunting grounds. Following this approach, it would take the FVS at least ten years to verify the implementation of the biosecurity requirements in all the hunting grounds, which limits the effectiveness of these official controls. The audit team verified a sample of official controls carried out on hunting grounds, which all had storage rooms and where hunters kept the carcases in them until the laboratory results were available. The FVS confirmed that all hunting grounds inspected so far had been in compliance with these requirements.

The official control on the handling and storage of wild boar carcases in general and on the destruction of carcases resulted positive to ASF in particular has improved since the FVS became responsible for this control in 2019. However, its efficiency is limited until official controls are more representative.

citations.text: The objective of the State Forest Service for the current hunting season is to inspect 1,200 hunting grounds (they had inspected around 1,000 so far this season). Inspections are unannounced and, contrary to a legal requirement in force a few years ago, hunters do not have to inform the State Forest Service offices in advance of when they plan to hunt. For this reason, and according to the information provided to the audit team, inspectors have not been able to perform their tasks in half of the visits, as no hunting activities were taking place. In addition, inspections do not target any specific species so only in approximately 300 out of the 1,000 inspections wild boar was being hunted.

According to the State Forest Service, when wild boar is being hunted, inspectors must focus on biosecurity aspects. These are, for example, checking the presence of disinfectant at the point of hunting, the burial of offal if wild boars are gutted on the spot or the transport of offal to a watertight container or that carcases do not get in contact. However, inspectors have not received any specific training on biosecurity and there are no instructions or guidelines available to them.

The State Forest Service has prepared a checklist for the inspections, but it does not contain any detail on the biosecurity aspects checked (only yes/no). There is an online application to report the inspection results, but it does not contain details on the species that were hunted during the inspection therefore there is no overview of the wild boar hunting grounds visited. The State Forest Service assumed that there was hunting of wild boar if biosecurity was reported.

According to the data contained in the online application, inspectors have never found any non-compliance on biosecurity. An inspector clarified that although not reported, in cases of shortcomings, they normally prefer to instruct hunters to improve their awareness regarding biosecurity. 8 5.1.4 Control of ABPs of domestic and feral pigs Legal requirements Articles 2, 7 and 10 of Decision 2014/709/EU. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control point plans.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: In all of the establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in three of the six establishments. In these cases, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was inadequate or very generic without the level of detail necessary for appropriate hazard identification and consequent risk assessment. In one establishment, the FeBO identified some critical control points in its own hazard analyses. However, the audit team noted that the established 4 critical limits and operator`s monitoring producers were not adequate for these critical control points, and therefore were not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling for residues is targeted, unannounced to the operator, and takes into account the risk criteria laid down in EU legislation.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 9(1) and (4) of Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Article 2(2) and Annexes II and III to Regulation (EU) 2022/1644.

citations.text: The selection of holdings to be sampled is within the competence of each TSU office, which decides on the farms and establishments to be sampled. Sampling was assigned well in advance to farms and establishments randomly chosen from those planned for various routine inspections during the month. Production volumes, previous non- compliant test results, the outcome of previous routine inspections on farms, quality parameters of raw milk, change of activity type of the operators/farms, etc., are factors which are not considered in the planning, however. This is not in line with applicable EU requirements (21). Conclusions on planning of residue monitoring

In the three TSUs visited, sampling was in most of the cases examined neither targeted nor performed without prior notice being given to the operator. Most of the samples were taken randomly by food inspectors (at slaughterhouses and from honey) and by veterinary inspectors (for eggs, milk, fish). This is not in line with EU requirements (25).

While national procedures clearly state that, in line with applicable EU legal requirements (26), RCP samples can only be taken by trained and authorised sampling officers, this was not always the case. In one TSU, samples were regularly taken by official veterinarians engaged in ante- and post-mortem inspection at slaughter. Whilst these veterinarians were likely capable of carrying out the sampling correctly, they had not been trained for the task. This is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (27).

Contrary to applicable EU requirements (21), the choice of animals to be sampled was not risk-based but random with no justification given. For aquaculture finfish, sampling was carried out exclusively at processing plants on fish ready to be placed on the market and not at all stages of production, as required by EU legislation, which stipulates that, for Group A (illegal) substances, samples must be taken from fish at all stages of farming (28).

The audit team noted that, in two visited TSUs, sometimes it happened that a single sample taken was registered in the records as several individual samples that were originally planned. Therefore, the number of samples actually collected was lower than the number indicated in the plan.

In general, the RCP is implemented as planned. The majority of samples however, are taken with prior notice being given to the operators and in many cases are selected randomly, rather than being targeted as required by EU legislation and national legal requirements. Collectively these shortcomings in implementation weaken the effectiveness of residues controls.

citations.text: In the three TSUs visited, there were delays in the identification of non-compliances. In one case (up to one year after having received the result), the non-compliance (chloramphenicol) was overlooked by the inspector in charge. It was discovered by the central competent authority in the framework of result collection and transmission to the European Food Safety Authority. The FVS has a formal agreement (42) with BIOR describing the arrangements for, inter alia, carrying out laboratory testing for the official controls on the food chain which includes controls on residues. To ensure that structure and equipment of primary production fishing vessels enable hygienic handling of fishery products in order to comply with the requirements set in part I, points (A)(1) and (2) of Chapter I, Section VIII of

citations.text: The FVS maintains its own list of primary production fishing vessels despite the existence of a list of commercial fishing vessels maintained by the Ministry of Agriculture. Registration with the latter is a pre-requisite to obtain a fishing licence, but not the registration with the FVS. The audit team noted that the FVS procedure in place for registration of fishing vessels does not require the verification of the information available (i.e., by cross-checking with information held on the list of the Ministry of Agriculture or the EU fleet register). The system relies on the operators' application for registration, which, in some cases, may never come. Therefore, the procedure does not allow the CA to obtain readily available information to ensure the completeness of the lists in line with the requirement in point 1(b) of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and thus reliably identify all fishing vessels that should be included in the scope of official controls.

In this respect, the audit team noted some discrepancies between the FVS's lists and the list of the Latvian fishing vessels included in the EU fishing fleet register. The audit team also noted that a fishing vessel, which was included only in the EU fishing fleet register, but not in the CA's list, engaged in commercial fishing activities recorded in the Latvian Fisheries Integrated Control and Information System (LZIKIS) of the Ministry of Agriculture, primarily used by the State Environmental Service.

The audit team noted that the form used by operators for applying for approval of their vessels does not require details about the vessel's characteristics (e.g., gross tonnage, length etc.). The application form used is the same, both for approvals and registrations. Furthermore, the approval procedure does not require, either the direct consultation of the EU fishing fleet register, or the Ministry of Agriculture to obtain information, that would allow the CA to assess the veracity or correctness of an application in accordance to point 2 of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

The audit team noted that, based on the information available in the EU fishing fleet register, one vessel on the FVS's list for primary production fishing vessels, was one of the biggest vessels of the Latvian fleet and had the same characteristics (length and gross tonnage, engine power, fishing gear etc.) as one of the approved freezer vessels (a sister vessel). Based on further information collected, the vessel produces without an approval, 5 frozen fishery products, which are then landed in a third country in packages without bearing an identification mark.

With regard to vessels (fishing, freezer and factory vessels), weaknesses were noted in the registration and approval procedures as these can start operation without having been registered or approved with the CA and remain out of the scope of official controls (contrary to the requirements in national legislation).

audits.title: Safety of milk and dairy products

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of food business operators' compliance regarding procedures based on HACCP principles, as laid down in Regulation (EC) Nos 852/2004, 853/2004 and 2073/2005, (in particular, in relation to microbiological criteria) are effective as required by Article 8.1. of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In general, the findings in the inspection reports reflected the situation regarding the HACCP-based procedures. Nevertheless, in some of the establishments visited, the audit team detected deficiencies in relation to these plans (including the prerequisite pro- grammes) which were not mentioned in the inspection reports. For example: in some es- tablishments HACCP plans were not updated by the FBO (e.g. alkaline phosphatase test used for heat-treatment verification but the HACCP plan contained peroxidase test; flowchart was not updated regarding re-work); discrepancy between the time/temperature values of pasteurisation in the HACCP plan and the actual values used; no mention in the plan that certain processes require time separation; layout plan of the establishment did not include all the cold storage facilities; pest control plans were in- complete (lack of evidence of bait maps and monitoring of rodent activity).

In most of the establishments visited by the audit team that were manufacturing ready- to-eat (RTE) dairy products, environmental sampling carried out by the FBOs to detect the possible presence of Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes) did not follow the European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) guidelines on sampling the food pro- cessing area and equipment for detection of this pathogen (in particular, sampling of en- vironment should also take place during processing). In the establishments visited this sampling was carried out after cleaning and disinfection (before processing) only. In one of the establishments visited manufacturing RTE products, the FBO's own-check sam- pling plan did not include any environmental (i.e. processing areas and equipment) sam- pling for the detection of L. monocytogenes. This is not in line with Article 5(2) of Reg- ulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The above-mentioned shortcomings had not been detected by the CAs during official controls and audits. A CCA representative confirmed to the audit team that this specific issue with environmental sampling for Listeria has not been checked during official con- trols.

In one of the establishments visited, cottage cheese was not tested for all the microbio- logical parameters required by Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (i.e. it was not tested for coagulase-positive staphylococci and Escherichia coli). This non-compliance was not detected during official controls. The audit team noted that, in general, the own-control sampling frequency for food pathogens was low in the smaller capacity establishments (one sample annually per product) and often consisted of only one sample unit instead of the five required in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005; in this regard, no dero- gation (based on Article 5 of this Regulation) had been granted by FVS to the FBOs.

The official controls did not cover FBOs' compliance with procedures, based on HACCP principles in sufficient depth, in particular, regarding microbiological criteria, and therefore did not identify all relevant shortcomings.
